questions.stem: Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank: 'The teacher distributed the question papers ___ all the students in the classroom.'
questions.explanation: 'Among' is used when referring to more than two people or things. 'Between' is used for exactly two. Since papers were distributed to an entire class (multiple students), 'among' is correct. 'Around' and 'with' do not collocate with 'distributed' here.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank: 'Neither Ram ___ Shyam attended the morning assembly.'
questions.explanation: 'Neither...nor' is the fixed correlative conjunction pair. 'Neither...and' and 'neither...or' are grammatically incorrect. 'Neither...but' is not a standard pair. Correct: 'Neither Ram nor Shyam attended the assembly.'
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank: 'Despite ___ hard for six months, she could not clear the competitive examination.'
questions.explanation: After 'Despite' (a preposition), a gerund (V+ing) must be used, not a bare infinitive or finite verb. 'Despite studying' is correct. 'Despite study', 'Despite studied', and 'Despite to study' are all grammatically wrong.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank: 'He was accused ___ misusing his official position for personal gain.'
questions.explanation: The fixed preposition after 'accuse' is 'of'. One is accused of a crime/offence, not 'for', 'in', or 'about'. Similarly: suspected of, convicted of, guilty of. Correct: 'He was accused of misusing his position.'
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank: 'The revised salary structure ___ into effect from the first of next month.'
questions.explanation: 'Come into effect' is a fixed collocation meaning to become operative or valid. 'Gets into effect', 'brings into effect', and 'puts into effect' are not standard fixed expressions for this meaning. Correct: 'The revised structure comes into effect from next month.'
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank: 'The senior judge ___ over the hearing and read out the final verdict.'
questions.explanation: 'Preside over' is the standard collocation for a judge or authority figure formally conducting proceedings. 'Chair' is used for meetings/committees. 'Directed' and 'supervised' do not collocate with 'over' in a legal-proceeding context. Correct: 'presided over the hearing'.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank: 'Most children in this age group prefer playing outdoors ___ watching television.'
questions.explanation: The standard structure for 'prefer' is 'prefer X to Y'. When comparing two activities, 'to' is the correct preposition. 'Prefer...than' is incorrect; 'prefer...over' is informal American English; 'instead' cannot substitute the preposition here.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank: 'All employees are expected to ___ strictly to the company's code of conduct.'
questions.explanation: 'Adhere to' is the precise formal collocation for strictly following rules or guidelines. 'Follow' does not take 'to' (you follow rules directly). 'Conform to' works but implies adjusting to a pattern. 'Comply to' is wrong (correct is 'comply with'). 'Adhere to' is the exact fit.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank: 'The principal ___ the students to task for their disruptive behaviour during the examination.'
questions.explanation: 'Take someone to task' is a fixed idiom meaning to reprimand or criticize someone firmly. 'Put to task', 'set to task', and 'give to task' are not standard expressions. Correct: 'The principal took the students to task.'
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank: 'The manager believed ___ rewarding employees who showed initiative and dedication.'
questions.explanation: 'Believe in' is the fixed preposition when expressing faith, trust, or the practice of something (believe in hard work, believe in justice). 'Believe at', 'believe on', and 'believe about' are not standard collocations in this context.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank: 'After years of struggle, the young singer finally ___ into the competitive entertainment industry.'
questions.explanation: 'Break into' is a phrasal verb meaning to successfully enter a competitive or difficult field. 'Entered into' does not capture the sense of overcoming barriers. 'Stepped into' implies replacing someone. 'Pushed into' suggests force from outside. 'Broke into' is the precise idiom.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank: 'Study hard ___ you should fail the examination and regret your carelessness later.'
questions.explanation: 'Lest' means 'for fear that' and is followed by 'should + V1'. The structure 'lest...should' expresses a precaution against an undesired event. 'So that' requires a positive purpose clause. 'Because' gives a reason, not a precaution. Correct: 'Study hard lest you should fail.'
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank: 'Exhausted after the long journey, she ___ down on the sofa and fell asleep instantly.'
questions.explanation: 'Lay' is the Simple Past of the intransitive verb 'lie' (to recline). 'Laid' is the Simple Past of the transitive verb 'lay' (to place something). Since the sentence means she reclined, the correct past tense is 'lay'. 'Lain' is the past participle; 'lie' is the present form.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank: 'You cannot enter the examination hall ___ you produce your valid admit card.'
questions.explanation: 'Unless' means 'except if' or 'if not' and introduces a negative condition. The sentence means: entry is not permitted if you do NOT have the admit card. 'Unless' fits perfectly. 'If' creates a positive condition. 'Until' implies time. 'Although' implies concession.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the most appropriate phrase to fill in the blank: 'He cannot even speak Hindi properly, ___ write an essay in it.'
questions.explanation: 'Let alone' is used after a negative statement to introduce something even more difficult or extreme. 'He cannot speak Hindi, let alone write an essay' — if speaking is beyond him, writing is even more so. 'Never mind' is informal. 'Much less' also works but is slightly less common in formal usage. 'Let alone' is the most natural and SSC-tested choice.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank: 'She is very good ___ painting landscapes and has won several national awards.'
questions.explanation: 'Good at' is the standard preposition when referring to skill or ability in a specific activity. 'Good in' is used for broad subject areas (good in mathematics). 'Good on' and 'good for' do not apply here. Correct: 'She is very good at painting landscapes.'
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank: 'He passed the examination ___ studying for only two days before the test.'
questions.explanation: 'Despite' is a preposition and takes a noun or gerund directly: 'despite studying'. 'In spite' must be followed by 'of': 'in spite of studying' — option C is incomplete. 'Although' and 'even though' are conjunctions and require a clause (subject + verb), not a gerund phrase.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank: 'Without mentioning it directly, the speaker ___ to the recent controversy within the organisation.'
questions.explanation: 'Allude to' specifically means to make an indirect or passing reference to something without naming it explicitly. 'Refer to' implies a direct or explicit mention. 'Pointed to' implies indicating evidence. 'Indicated' is too vague. Since the speaker did NOT mention it directly, 'alluded' is the precise word.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank: 'Though he knew a great deal about the incident, he remained ___ and refused to share any details.'
questions.explanation: 'Reticent' specifically means unwilling to reveal information or speak about something — exactly the sense of knowing but not sharing. 'Silent' means not speaking at all. 'Reluctant' means unwilling to do something (broader). 'Reserved' is a general personality trait. 'Reticent' is the precise vocabulary match here.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank: 'The project was completed on time, ___ with some compromises on the original design.'
questions.explanation: 'Albeit' (= although/even though) is a conjunction used within a sentence to introduce a concessive phrase or clause: 'completed on time, albeit with compromises'. 'Although' and 'even though' need a full clause (subject + verb). 'However' and 'nevertheless' are connective adverbs used at the start of new clauses.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank: 'The eyewitness account helped to ___ the version of events presented by the defence team.'
questions.explanation: 'Corroborate' specifically means to strengthen or confirm a statement, theory, or finding with independent evidence or testimony — precisely the legal/investigative context here. 'Confirm' and 'verify' are more general. 'Support' is the weakest. 'Corroborate' is the most precise and exam-expected word.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank: 'She has been working at the same organisation ___ she completed her post-graduation.'
questions.explanation: 'Since' is used with Present Perfect/Past Perfect to indicate the point in time when an action began. 'She has been working since she completed her degree' = from that point until now. 'For' is used with a duration (for ten years). 'From' is used with simple tenses, not perfect continuous. 'After' does not anchor the duration.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank: 'The government plans to ___ the minimum wage for workers in the unorganised sector.'
questions.explanation: 'Raise' is a transitive verb meaning to increase or lift something. It takes an object ('raise the wage'). 'Rise' is intransitive (wages rise — no object). 'Arise' means to come up or occur. 'Arouse' means to stimulate or awaken. Only 'raise' can take 'the minimum wage' as its object.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank: 'The severe drought is expected to ___ millions of farmers across the riverine districts.'
questions.explanation: 'Affect' is the verb meaning to have an impact on or influence something. 'Effect' is primarily a noun (the effect); as a verb it means 'to bring about' (effect a change — rare). 'Influence' and 'impact' work but are less precise in formal contexts. 'Affect' is the standard choice in SSC-style fill-in-the-blank questions.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank: 'The new expressway was inaugurated ___ the Chief Minister in the presence of senior officials.'
questions.explanation: In passive constructions, the agent (the doer of the action) is introduced with 'by'. 'The expressway was inaugurated by the Chief Minister' — 'by' marks the agent. 'With' indicates an instrument/tool. 'Through' means via a medium. 'From' indicates source or origin.
questions.subject: English
